clips.title: Kubernetes Network Policies Explained
clips.why: Viktor shows what a NetworkPolicy is and then what really happens without one: any application can reach any other.
look: Without policies, a pod in one namespace calls a database in another one, and nothing stops it. That is n8n reaching our broker.
Policies select pods by label, not by name or IP, so they keep working when pods are replaced.
The default changes only for the pods a policy selects.
clips.after: The broker's policy turns his open cluster into one where only the orchestrator worker reaches the internal port.

clips.title: Kubernetes Network Policy Tutorial - yaml explained + Demo Calico
clips.why: The trap that makes a policy only look like a wall: without a network plugin that enforces it, nothing happens.
look: He applies a policy and the traffic still flows, because no policy agent is installed.
After installing a plugin that enforces policies, the same test is refused.
The test itself: a call from a pod that should fail, before and after.
clips.after: That is why our policies are not done at kubectl apply: a probe from a refused pod and from the allowed pod proves the wall on inf.

clips.title: Back to Basics: Providing Secure Connectivity with SaaS Applications with PrivateLink
clips.why: AWS explains the provider and consumer sides of PrivateLink, and why it exposes one service instead of a whole network.
look: The provider puts a Network Load Balancer in front of its service and publishes it as an endpoint service.
The consumer gets an endpoint with private addresses in its own network; the two networks are never joined.
The provider decides which accounts may connect.
clips.after: Here inf is the provider, with three listeners, and the ai-agents account, where the sandbox VMs live, is the only allowed consumer.

practice.q: A cluster has no NetworkPolicies at all. Can a pod in the n8n namespace open a connection to the broker in ai-agents?

options.why: A namespace groups objects and their names, but it is not a network wall.

options.text: Yes, every pod can reach every pod until a policy selects the target
options.why: That open default is exactly why the broker needs a policy of its own.

options.text: Only if the broker's Service is of type LoadBalancer
options.why: A ClusterIP Service is reachable from every pod in the cluster. ClusterIP only keeps the outside world away.

practice.q: Finish the rule so that only the orchestrator worker may connect to the broker.
practice.hint: The label of the one service allowed to open runs.
practice.why: The rule allows pods by label. Any pod without app=orchestrator-worker is refused, in this namespace or any other.

practice.q: A Service listens on port 7233 and sends traffic to the pod's port 80. Which port goes in the NetworkPolicy rule?

options.why: The policy is checked at the pod, after the Service has changed the port. A rule for 7233 matches nothing, so everyone is refused.
NetworkPolicies talk about pods, so the port is the container's port. Naming the port in the Deployment avoids this mix-up.

options.text: Both, or the policy is invalid
options.why: One is enough, and the right one is the pod's port.

practice.q: Put the steps of adding a policy to inf in the right order.
items: Write the policy in the service's unit, with selectors by label
Run a plan and get the pull request reviewed
Probe from a pod that should be refused, and see it refused
Probe from the pod that should pass, and see it still works
practice.why: A policy is a request to the network plugin. It is only a wall once both probes behave as expected.

practice.q: A sandbox VM tries to call the broker's internal port. What stops it?

options.text: The broker's NetworkPolicy, because the VM is not labelled orchestrator-worker
options.why: The VM is not a pod, so it never gets as far as the cluster's policies.

options.text: That port is not one of the three PrivateLink listeners, so from the VM it does not exist
options.why: The VM's network has no route to inf except the endpoint, and the endpoint only offers the broker's sandbox port, the gateway and the collector.

options.text: The egress proxy, which blocks every port except 443
options.why: The proxy controls the way to the internet. Traffic to inf does not go through it; it goes through PrivateLink.
